notesStmt.note: This is one of many similar corrected proof slips of this poem. Horace Traubel notes in With Walt Whitman in Camden that although Whitman was in the practice of having poems "set up for private distribution [i.e., to friends and admirers] at the printing office of Henry Curtz," he never gave out the slips until the poems had been published ([Boston: Small, Maynard & Company, 1906] 1:180). This proof slip therefore probably dates to shortly after the poem's first appearance in November 1889.
A corrected proof slip of "My 71st Year," which was first published in The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine in November 1889. The poem lwas ater reprinted in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891).

lg.head: MY 71ST YEAR.
lg.l: With all their chances, changes, losses, sorrows,

My parents' deaths, the vagaries of my life, the many tearing
passions of me, ‸the war of '63 and '4,

As some old broken soldier, after a long, hot wearying march,
or haply after battle,

At twilight, hobbling, answering yet to company roll-call, Here,
with vital voice,
Reporting yet, saluting yet the Officer over all.
